subject: Climate & Environment
title: Pollinators and Food Chains
description: A short lesson to help you apply Pollinators and Food Chains.

hook.text: One out of every three bites of food you eat was made possible by a pollinator.

buildup.text: Bees, butterflies, bats, and birds carry pollen between flowers, enabling fruit and seed.

discovery.text: Without pollinators, coffee, chocolate, almonds, and most fruits would disappear.

twist.text: Colony collapse disorder wiped out 30-40% of US honeybee colonies in a single year.

climax.text: Neonicotinoid pesticides disorient bees — they can't find their way home.

punchline.text: No bees, no fruit. It really is that simple.

quiz.question: What fraction of food depends on pollinators?

details.summary: Bees, butterflies, bats, and other pollinators enable reproduction in over 75 percent of flowering plants and 35 percent of global food crops. Pollinator decline from pesticides, habitat loss, and disease threatens food security for billions.
details.whyItMatters: Without pollinators, much of the food supply collapses. The pollinator crisis is an early warning that industrial agriculture is undermining its own foundation.
takeaways: Seventy-five percent of crops benefit from animal pollination
Neonicotinoid pesticides impair bee navigation and reproduction
Wild pollinators often outperform managed honeybees

faq.question: What is causing pollinator populations to decline?
faq.answer: The main drivers are habitat loss, pesticide exposure especially neonicotinoids, disease and parasites like the Varroa mite, climate change altering bloom timing, and light pollution disrupting nocturnal pollinators.

faq.question: What would happen if all pollinators disappeared?
faq.answer: Roughly a third of food crops would produce little or no fruit, including apples, almonds, coffee, and chocolate. Wild plant reproduction would collapse, triggering cascading losses through entire ecosystems.
